subject: Biotechnology
title: PCR: Copying DNA
description: A quick win: understand PCR: Copying DNA.

hook.text: Kary Mullis invented PCR while driving on a California highway in 1983 — an idea worth a Nobel Prize.

buildup.text: PCR copies a specific DNA segment by heating, cooling, and extending — doubling the amount each cycle.

discovery.text: After 30 cycles, one DNA molecule becomes over a billion copies — exponential amplification in hours.

twist.text: The key was Taq polymerase from hot-spring bacteria — it survives the 95°C heating step that kills normal enzymes.

climax.text: PCR drives forensics, diagnostics, and research — COVID tests, paternity tests, and crime labs all depend on it.

punchline.text: One molecule becomes a billion — PCR is biotech's photocopier.

quiz.question: Why is Taq polymerase essential for PCR?
options: It copies DNA faster than any other enzyme
It survives the high temperatures needed to separate DNA strands during each cycle
It was the first enzyme ever discovered in a laboratory

details.summary: PCR amplifies a specific DNA segment millions of times in hours using repeated cycles of heating to separate strands, cooling to bind primers, and extending with heat-stable polymerase. It makes enough DNA from trace samples for analysis, sequencing, or cloning.
details.whyItMatters: PCR is arguably the most important technique in molecular biology. It enables DNA forensics from a single hair, pathogen detection from a nasal swab, and genetic research from minuscule tissue samples, earning Kary Mullis the 1993 Nobel Prize.
takeaways: PCR amplifies specific DNA sequences through repeated thermal cycling
Each cycle doubles the target DNA, producing millions of copies in hours
Kary Mullis won the 1993 Nobel Prize for inventing PCR

faq.question: How does PCR amplify DNA so rapidly?
faq.answer: Each cycle doubles the target DNA: 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, 16, and so on exponentially. After 30 cycles, one molecule becomes over a billion copies. The process takes just a few hours in an automated thermal cycler machine.

faq.question: What made PCR possible as a practical technique?
faq.answer: The discovery of Taq polymerase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus was essential. This heat-stable enzyme survives the 95-degree denaturation step in each cycle. Before Taq, fresh enzyme had to be manually added after every heating step.
